Nothing proves a real email produces one.

WHAT IS COVERED, so this bead is not overstated:
- RulePlanner as a mechanism has unit tests: internal/daemon/planner_test.go's TestRulePlanner and TestNewRulePlanner_InvalidRegex.
- cmd/beadle-daemon/main_test.go covers owner-key resolution, command loading, and the stale-pipeline sweep.

WHAT IS NOT COVERED:
The daemon's actual planner configuration lives as a hardcoded literal in cmd/beadle-daemon/main.go:136-143:

    rules := []daemon.RuleEntry{{
        Pattern: \"(?i)summarize|summary\",
        Commands: []daemon.CommandCall{{Command: \"summarize\", Args: map[string]any{\"text\": \"see email body\"}}},
    }}

That pattern is the sole thing deciding whether an incoming email reaches the x-gated execute path in production. Verified: the literal '(?i)summarize' appears in no test file anywhere in the repo. The 'summarize' hits in pipeline_edge_test.go are command *definitions*, not the pattern.

And the harness deliberately stubs the planner — internal/daemon/harness_test.go:138 uses daemon.StubPlanner with a fixed result — so the tier never exercises pattern matching at all.

CONSEQUENCE: change or break that regex and every gate test still passes. The tier would report green while no email could trigger anything. That is the same shape as the defect the tier was built to catch (beadle-8gt: a path that had never actually run), one layer up — the gates are proven, their trigger is not.

Stubbing the planner in the harness was the right call and should stay: the four gates are what that test is for, and coupling them to regex behavior would make failures ambiguous. The missing piece is separate coverage that the daemon's real wiring, as configured in main.go, produces the expected plan for a representative email.

Also worth considering while here: the pattern being a hardcoded literal rather than configuration means an operator cannot change what triggers their daemon without recompiling. That may be deliberate (it is adjacent to the zero-agent-authority posture — see beadle-tl6 for the planner-authority question) but it is undocumented either way.

tool_input.content:
beadle-daemon: intended design vs. what is real

What the docs promise, what the code actually does, and the shortest honest path between them.

Generated 2026-08-31 · main at 14aa9ba · every claim below was checked against source, not recalled

real works, and something proves it partial works with a stated gap absent promised somewhere, no implementation

01The pipeline, stage by stage

This is the path an inbound email takes. Until 2026-08-30 it had been run end to end roughly three times, all by hand. The first automated run of it found four defects.

1
Poll the mailbox internal/email/poller.go
First poll never fires the callback, by design, so a restart does not reprocess the backlog. Minimum interval 1m.
real
2
Classify transport trust handler.go:160 · verifyTrust
Four levels. Only Verified (real GPG signature, isolated keyring) and Trusted (Proton end-to-end) are accepted.
Gap: Trusted rests entirely on two headers, safe only because Proton Bridge sets them and Bridge is assumed to be on localhost. Nothing verifies that. The code says so itself — TODO(beadle-xxx): verify IMAP is localhost — and that placeholder ID was never filed. Now beadle-hv7i.
partial
3
Check per-contact x permission handler.go:149 · contacts.CheckPermission
Independent of trust. A perfectly signed message from an ungranted sender unlocks nothing. Today exactly one contact holds x.
real
4
Turn the email into a plan planner.go · configured at cmd/beadle-daemon/main.go:136
RulePlanner matches a regex against subject and body and emits a fixed command call. The mechanism is unit-tested.
Gap: the production rule is a hardcoded literal — "(?i)summarize|summary" — and appears in no test anywhere. The harness stubs the planner, correctly, so the tier proves the gates given a plan and never that an email produces one. Break that regex and every gate test still passes. beadle-ivtd.
Absent: LLMPlanner is a stub. Trusted, permitted mail cannot author a plan — it can only select from pre-signed recipes. beadle-tl6.
partial
5
Load and verify the recipe command.go · signature.go
Real GPG verification against the configured authorizer key, in an isolated keyring. Unsigned, wrong-key, and expired-key files are rejected. An absent or ambiguous daemon.json disables command loading entirely rather than falling back to unsigned.
Sharp edge: that zero-commands default lives in main.go, not in the library. daemon.LoadCommands with an empty ownerKeyID loads unsigned — the invariant is enforced by the caller, so a second caller would not inherit it.
real
6
Build the mission contract and create the mission pipeline.go · mission.go · real ethos CLI
Fixed 2026-08-30. It had emitted inputs.args and inputs.pipeline_output, which ethos strict-rejects, so every daemon-triggered mission failed here. Nobody had noticed because nothing had run it.
real
7
Spawn the worker spawner.go
Real claude subprocess with an explicit env allowlist, capped turns and budget, and a narrowed PATH.
Gap: no OS-level sandbox. TODO: container isolation (network namespace, seccomp) at spawner.go:109 is unfiled and unbeaded.
partial
8
Record the job, reply, clean up persist.go · pipeline.go
Jobs are written to disk with atomic rename; a crash-interrupted job is marked failed on restart; records are pruned after 30 days by a ticker. All landed 2026-08-30/31 — before that, save() was a no-op and the recovery scan always read an empty directory.
real

02The four documented invariants

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md lists these as design invariants. Three hold. One is a claim with no code behind it.

InvariantStatusReality
Zero agent authority
every executed command is signed		 partial True for execution. But OnNewMail creates the mission record and starts the pipeline goroutine on trust + permission alone, with no signed command in that decision. With zero commands loaded nothing downstream runs, so it is currently harmless — the record is still created unconditionally. Documented in ARCHITECTURE.md as a known gap.
Preflight before execute real Args validated before any command runs; no partial execution.
Isolated verification real Inbound and recipe signature checks each run in their own temporary GNUPGHOME. An untrusted key never touches the system keyring.
Expired / non-expiring keys rejected real Enforced on the primary key and any signing-capable subkey.
Audit log is tamperproof
append-only, GPG-signed		 absent There is no audit log. Grep for it in internal/daemon returns four comments mentioning the word and zero implementation. The pipeline records added this week are operational state, not a signed audit trail — they are mutable and unsigned. beadle-623.

The one to be honest about

A document promising a tamperproof, GPG-signed, append-only audit log, with nothing behind it, is worse than silence: it invites someone to rely on a control that does not exist. Either build it or move the claim out of the invariants list and into a roadmap. Both are fine; leaving it as an invariant is not.

03Can a new operator actually use this?

No. This is the largest practical gap and it is not a code defect.

A fresh install runs zero commands, by design, with no way out

The daemon refuses to load recipes unless ~/.punt-labs/beadle/daemon.json names an authorizer key and each recipe carries that key's signature. That default is correct — it is the zero-agent-authority posture.

But no tooling exists to reach the configured state. There is no beadle init and no beadle sign in either binary — verified. An operator must hand-write daemon.json, then hand-craft a canonical-subset signature over each recipe by replicating what internal/daemon does internally. In practice that means the daemon is operable by someone who reads the source. Tracked as beadle-7gm.

04What the new test tier does and does not prove

Merged 2026-08-31 in PR #261. It runs identically under make check and in CI, with no t.Skip anywhere in internal/daemon.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Trust classification admits only Verified/Trustedreal Negative case fails when the guard is disabled — verified by patching handler.go:162 to if false: "should have 0 item(s), but has 1"
Ungranted sender unlocks nothingreal Fails when perm.Execute is disabled
Unsigned / wrong-key / expired recipes rejectedreal Fails when the NO_PUBKEY case is broken
Contract accepted by the real ethos CLIreal Plus a negative control that fails when the malformed contract is made valid
A real email produces a planabsent Planner is stubbed; the production regex is untested. beadle-ivtd
The Store wiring writes a recordabsent The harness passes nil for the store, so the line executes unasserted. beadle-fbhp
No test mutates real ethos statereal Tree hash byte-identical across a full -race run

The tier's best evidence is that it caught its own bugs

Within minutes of first running in CI it found three violations of its own premise: a symlink to the developer's global archetypes tree, make test not putting the installed binary on PATH, and a GOPATH expression that breaks on multi-entry values.

None were findable from the authoring machine, because that is precisely the environment in which none of them reproduce. For a change whose whole premise is dev/CI parity, local validation was the weakest available signal. Recorded as DES-036.

05The path to real

Ordered by what unblocks the most, not by size. The first two are the difference between "a developer can demo this" and "an operator can run it."

  1. Make the trust story honest — beadle-hv7i (P2) Verify IMAP is loopback before honoring Proton-origin headers, or refuse to classify as Trusted. Right now one of the two accepted trust levels rests on an unverified environmental assumption that the code itself flags. Cheapest security fix on the list, and the test tier makes the negative case easy.
  2. Give an operator a way in — beadle-7gm (P3, misprioritized) beadle init and beadle sign. Without these the daemon is unusable by anyone who has not read internal/daemon. This is P3 and should not be; it gates every other daemon capability from a user's perspective.
  3. Close the trigger gap — beadle-ivtd (P3) Assert that the daemon's real wiring produces a plan for a representative email. Keep the harness's stub planner — that separation is correct. This is separate coverage, not a change to the tier.
  4. Resolve the audit-log claim — beadle-623 (P3) Build it or demote it out of the invariants list. An unimplemented invariant is a liability in a document people are told to trust.
  5. Cover the persistence wiring — beadle-fbhp (P2) Now cheap: the fixtures exist. Pass a real store into the harness and assert a record reaches disk. Then remove the wiring line and confirm the test fails.
  6. Decide on worker sandboxing — unfiled spawner.go:109's container-isolation TODO has no bead. The worker runs with a narrowed env and PATH but no namespace or seccomp confinement. Either file it with a decision or record why the current confinement is sufficient.
  7. Then, and only then, LLMPlanner — beadle-tl6 (P3) Letting trusted mail author a plan removes the "it can only pick from pre-signed recipes" safety property. It needs its own authorization story, and it should land after the trust and audit gaps above are closed rather than before.

One thing this artifact is not

A verdict on beadle-email. That path — an agent with a mailbox, reading and replying under r/w grants — has real usage behind it and works. Everything above is about beadle-daemon, the x-gated recipe runner, which had been exercised about three times before this week. The two share a trust model and almost nothing else.

How to check this document rather than trust it. Every status above was read from source at 14aa9ba. The bead IDs are live: bd show <id>. The invariants list is docs/ARCHITECTURE.md. The tier is internal/daemon/harness_test.go.

Deliberately contains no counts of files, tests, or defect sites. An earlier document in this repo carried a count that was wrong by more than three times, survived two review rounds, and was copied twice before anyone ran the command that would have checked it.
